# BAckground and justification 

novel cross-sectional claim count models for vehicle insurance built upon the combinedd actuarial neural network (CANN) framework proposed by Wüthrich and Merz. The CANN approach combines a classical actuarial model, such as a generalized linear model, with a neural network. This blending of models results in a two-component model comprising a classical regression model and a neural network part. 

The CANN model leverages the strengths of both components, providing a solid foundation and interpretability from the classical model while harnessing the flexibility and capacity to capture intricate relationships and interactions offered by the neural network. In our proposed models, we use well-known log-linear claim count regression models for the classical regression part and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) for the neural network part. The MLP part is used to process telematics car driving data given as a vector characterizing the driving behavior of each insured driver. 

Reproduction of the cross-sectional models of Duval, Boucher & Pigeon (2024), fit on
the public So, Boucher & Valdez (2021) synthetic telematics portfolio.
The objectif is to compare and constrast the predictive and interpretatbility of 
- a glm model 
- a glm model + a neural network layer to model the non ,linearity of telematrics

exposure and frequency graph  by variable(age , sex ,carAge, Credit scoreYears no claims  )

```{r expo_freq plot function}

plot_freq_expo <- function(data, var, var_categorical) {
  
  summary_df <- data %>%
    group_by(.data[[var]], .data[[var_categorical]]) %>%
    summarise(
      Exposure = sum(Exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
      Claims = sum(NB_Claim, na.rm = TRUE),
      Frequency = Claims / Exposure,
      .groups = "drop"
    )
  
  max_expo <- max(summary_df$Exposure, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  ggplot(summary_df,
         aes(x = .data[[var]],
             colour = .data[[var_categorical]],
             fill = .data[[var_categorical]])) +
    
    geom_col(
      aes(y = Exposure),
      position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
      alpha = 0.5
    ) +
    
    geom_line(
      aes(
        y = Frequency * max_expo,
        group = .data[[var_categorical]]
      ),
      linewidth = 1.2
    ) +
    
    
    scale_y_continuous(
      name = "Exposure",
      sec.axis = sec_axis(
        ~ . / max_expo,
        name = "Frequency"
      )
    ) +
    
    labs(
      title = paste("Exposure and Frequency by", var),
      x = var,
      colour = var_categorical,
      fill = var_categorical
    ) +
    
    theme_minimal()
}
```

### 3.2 CATEGORICAL VARIABLES 
 look at the exposure and frequency by caetgorical variables int he

```{r cat-freq}
categorical_vars <- c("Insured.sex", "Marital", "Region", "Car.use")
freq_by_cat <- function(v, data = dt) {
  data[, .(Exposure = sum(Exposure), Claims = sum(NB_Claim)), by = v][
    , Frequency := Claims / Exposure][order(-Exposure)]
}
for (v in categorical_vars) { cat("\n--", v, "--\n"); print(freq_by_cat(v)) }

```
- we are more exposed to male policyholders, we have more claims for males, yet lower frequency, so everything else held constant , male have less frequencies

- we have about twice the exposure to married people, and they have lower frequencies ceteris paribus

- We have about 4 times the exposure to Urban regions, and they have higher frequencies ceteris parisbus

- Farmers have the lowest frequency, and commute have the highest frequency, but we have too low exposure to commercial and farmer which may affect our models performance and prudence we will merge those two together as Commerial_farmer

```{r car use merging }
dt[, Car.use.grp := fifelse(
  Car.use %in% c("Commercial", "Farmer"),
  "Farmer_Commercial",
  Car.use
)]


dt[, Car.use.grp := factor(Car.use.grp)]
dt[, Car.use := NULL]
```

#### Fit Poissona nd NB 
```{r}
library(MASS)

# Parameters estimated from the data
lambda <- mean(dt$NB_Claim)

fit_nb <- fitdistr(dt$NB_Claim, "Negative Binomial")

size <- fit_nb$estimate["size"]
mu   <- fit_nb$estimate["mu"]
```

#### Combined Poisson vs NB comparison
```{r}
obs <- sort(dt$NB_Claim)

n <- length(obs)
# theorical poisson quantiles 
theo_pois <- qpois(
  ppoints(n),
  lambda = lambda
)
#theorical NB quantiles 
theo_nb <- qnbinom(
  ppoints(n),
  size = size,
  mu = mu
)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

qqplot(theo_pois, obs,
       main = "Poisson",
       pch = 19, col = "blue")
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)

qqplot(theo_nb, obs,
       main = "Negative Binomial",
       pch = 19, col = "darkgreen")
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```
we will now can compare:

Empirical distribution of NB_Claim
Fitted Poisson distribution
Fitted Negative Binomial distribution

on the same graph.(explique m=what is being done , )

#5 Model construction

## 5.1 Split the dataset into trainig and testing 
```{r split}
# new column that tells us if there is a claim or not 
dt[, HasClaim := as.integer(NB_Claim > 0)]

stratified_split <- function(n_idx, strata, p_train = 0.8, seed = 123) {
  set.seed(seed)
  parts <- lapply(split(n_idx, strata), function(idx) {
    idx <- sample(idx); n <- length(idx)
    n_tr <- floor(p_train * n)
    list(train = idx[seq_len(n_tr)],
         
         test  = idx[-seq_len(n_tr)])
  })
  list(train = unlist(lapply(parts, `[[`, "train"), use.names = FALSE),
       test  = unlist(lapply(parts, `[[`, "test"),  use.names = FALSE))
}
sp <- stratified_split(
seq_len(nrow(dt)),
dt$HasClaim,
p_train = 0.8
)
train_dt <- dt[sp$train]
test_dt <- dt[sp$test]

cat("rows:", nrow(train_dt), nrow(test_dt), "\n")
cat(
"claim rate by split:",
mean(train_dt$HasClaim),
mean(test_dt$HasClaim), "\n"
)
```

first we will construct two models 
```{r}
mod0 <- glm(
NB_Claim ~ 1,
family = poisson(),
offset = log(Exposure),
data = train_dt
)

mod1 <- MASS::glm.nb(
NB_Claim ~ offset(log(Exposure)),
data = train_dt
)
```

on observe une très forte correlations entre les variables telmatics. Nous allons 
les organiser en groupe de variables et calculer les colinearités intra groups puis vif poiur selectionner celles àn agrder dasn chasua egroupe de telematrics en focntion du ritère d'AIC

```{r}
family_best <- function(vars) {
  aics <- sapply(vars, function(v) {
    f <- reformulate(c(v, "offset(log(Exposure))"), response = "NB_Claim")
    AIC(glm.nb(f, data = train_dt)) # using NB distribution
  })
  names(which.min(aics))
}
# creating the telematics sub families 
accel_best <- family_best(c("Accel.06miles","Accel.08miles","Accel.09miles","Accel.11miles","Accel.12miles","Accel.14miles"))
brake_best <- family_best(c("Brake.06miles","Brake.08miles","Brake.09miles","Brake.11miles","Brake.12miles","Brake.14miles"))
lturn_best <- family_best(c("Left.turn.intensity08","Left.turn.intensity09","Left.turn.intensity10","Left.turn.intensity11","Left.turn.intensity12"))
rturn_best <- family_best(c("Right.turn.intensity08","Right.turn.intensity09","Right.turn.intensity10",
                            "Right.turn.intensity11","Right.turn.intensity12"))

pct_day_best <- family_best(c(
"Pct.drive.mon",
"Pct.drive.tue",
"Pct.drive.wed",
"Pct.drive.thr",
"Pct.drive.fri",
"Pct.drive.sat",
"Pct.drive.sun"))

pct_time_best <- family_best(c(
"Pct.drive.2hrs",
"Pct.drive.3hrs",
"Pct.drive.4hrs",
"Pct.drive.wkday",
"Pct.drive.wkend",
"Pct.drive.rush.am",
"Pct.drive.rush.pm"
))

selected_telematics <- c(
pct_day_best,
pct_time_best,
accel_best,
brake_best,
lturn_best,
rturn_best
)

selected_telematics
```
###  5.2.2 Catégoricals variables multicolinearity 
Nous pouvons  mesurer leur association avec le package DescTools using the cramers V ; what is it ? 
how does it work  
it calculate relationaship fobetween two variables, so we are trying to create a matric 
to find relationship between all varainles 

```{r}
cat_vars <- c(
"Insured.sex",
"Car.use.grp", 
"Marital", "Region"
)
cramer_mat <- matrix(
NA,
nrow = length(cat_vars),
ncol = length(cat_vars),
dimnames = list(cat_vars, cat_vars)
)
for (i in seq_along(cat_vars)) {
for (j in seq_along(cat_vars)) {
cramer_mat[i, j] <- CramerV(
train_dt[[cat_vars[i]]],
train_dt[[cat_vars[j]]]
)}}
round(cramer_mat, 3)
```
Good , there are weak multicolinearity between the categorical variables 
Now we calculate the final VIF on the complete model 
exlain vif vs gvif 
```{r vif }
final_variables = c(cat_vars, num_vars)
# comlete model 
form_vif <- as.formula(
  paste(
    "NB_Claim ~",
    paste(final_variables, collapse = " + "),
    "+ offset(log(Exposure))"))

mod_vif <- glm.nb(form_vif,data = train_dt)
v <- vif(mod_vif)
v

```
##5.3 Selection of variables 

```{r}
full_formula <- as.formula(
  paste(
    "NB_Claim ~",
    paste(final_variables, collapse = " + "),
    "+ offset(log(Exposure))" ))

mod_full_pois <- glm(
  full_formula,
  family = poisson(),
  data = train_dt
)

mod_full_nb <- MASS::glm.nb(
  full_formula,
  data = train_dt
)

AIC(mod0, mod_full_pois)
AIC(mod1, mod_full_nb)
```

```{r predicted_vs_observed frequencies }

plot_age_fit_plotly <- function(data, model) {

  data$pred <- predict(
    model,
    newdata = data,
    type = "response"
  )

  age_df <- data %>%
    group_by(Insured.age) %>%
    summarise(
      Exposure = sum(Exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
      Claims_obs = sum(NB_Claim, na.rm = TRUE),
      Claims_pred = sum(pred, na.rm = TRUE),
      Obs_Freq = Claims_obs / Exposure,
      Pred_Freq = Claims_pred / Exposure,
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  plot_ly() %>%

    add_bars(
      data = age_df,
      x = ~Insured.age,
      y = ~Exposure,
      name = "Exposure",
      marker = list(color = "skyblue"),
      opacity = 0.6,
      yaxis = "y"
    ) %>%

    add_lines(
      data = age_df,
      x = ~Insured.age,
      y = ~Obs_Freq,
      name = "Observed Frequency",
      line = list(
        color = "red",
        width = 3
      ),
      yaxis = "y2"
    ) %>%

    add_markers(
      data = age_df,
      x = ~Insured.age,
      y = ~Obs_Freq,
      name = "Observed Frequency",
      marker = list(
        color = "red",
        size = 6
      ),
      yaxis = "y2",
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) %>%

    add_lines(
      data = age_df,
      x = ~Insured.age,
```

# 7. Diagnostic o the errors of both models 

Given that we're predicting claim counts (NB_Claim) with an exposure offset, we will
compare (explain each metrics using math formulas ) :

- MAE # erreur aboslute moyenne
- RMSE # erreur quadratique moyenne 
- Poisson Deviance
- Distribution of residuals
- Observed vs Predicted frequencies

**1.Errors metrics calculations**
a function to calculate the errors metrics, given the predicted y and the observed yis

```{r calculate_errors_metrics}
eval_metrics <- function(y, pred) {
  mae <- mean(abs(y - pred))

  rmse <- sqrt(mean((y - pred)^2))

  poisson_dev <- 2 * sum(
    ifelse( y == 0,pred,y * log(y / pred) - (y - pred)))
# create a dataframe to store the errors 
  data.frame(MAE = mae, RMSE = rmse,PoissonDeviance = poisson_dev)
}
# metrics for the full model 
metrics_nb <- eval_metrics(test_dt$NB_Claim,test_dt$pred_nb)
# metrics for the step model 
metrics_step <- eval_metrics(test_dt$NB_Claim, test_dt$pred_nb_step)
# full metric
rbind(Full_NB = metrics_nb,Step_NB = metrics_step)
```

comparions and comments 

**2. Create residuals dataset**
```{r residuals}

comp_df <- test_dt %>%
  transmute(
    NB_Claim,

    resid_full =
      NB_Claim - pred_nb, # residuals errors using first full model 

    resid_step =
      NB_Claim - pred_nb_step, # residuals errors using second step model 

    abs_resid_full =
      abs(NB_Claim - pred_nb), # absolute values 

    abs_resid_step =
      abs(NB_Claim - pred_nb_step)
  )
```

**3. Boxplot of absolute errors**
```{r boxplot_abs_errors}
box_df <- comp_df %>%
  select(abs_resid_full,
         abs_resid_step) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(),  names_to = "Model",values_to = "AbsoluteError")

ggplot(box_df,aes(x = Model, y = AbsoluteError)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs( title = "Absolute Error Comparison",y = "Absolute Error")
```

# 8. CANN model 
here we build a neural network that will be initialsed with the glm and trained to 
understand the hiden non linear relationship hidden in the telematrics datasets 
The CANN blends a classical regression with a network by adding their linear predictors before the link: 

```
log( mu_i ) = log(exposure_i)                    <- offset
            + x_i^trad . beta                    <- log-linear (actuarial) part
            + MLP( x_i^trad , x_i^tele )         <- network (boosting) part
```
Two design decisions carry the whole idea and must not be skipped:
- The log-linear part receives ONLY traditional risk factors. It is deliberately constrained — it provides the stable, interpretable backbone.
- The MLP receives traditional AND telematics inputs, so it can learn interactions BETWEEN them, not just telematics effects in isolation. This is exactly what the paper argues a manually engineered feature set cannot do.

**Warm start**: β is initialised at GLM-A's fitted coefficients, and the MLP's output
layer is initialised at zero. At epoch 0 the CANN is numerically identical to GLM-A;
gradient descent can only move away from it in directions that improve the
likelihood.

## 8.1 Preparation des variables 
```{r}

# VARIABLES
trad_numeric <- c("Insured.age", "Car.age", "Credit.score", "Years.noclaims", "Annual.miles.drive")
trad_factors <- c("Insured.sex", "Marital", "Region", "Car.use.grp")

telematics_selected <- c(
  "Pct.drive.thr",
  "Pct.drive.rush.pm",
  "Accel.06miles",
  "Brake.06miles",
  "Left.turn.intensity08",
  "Right.turn.intensity10"
)

###################################################
# ALIGN FACTOR LEVELS
###################################################

for(v in trad_factors){

  train_dt[[v]] <- factor(train_dt[[v]])

  test_dt[[v]] <- factor(
    test_dt[[v]],
    levels = levels(train_dt[[v]])
  )
}

###################################################
# STANDARDIZATION PARAMETERS
###################################################

std_from_train <- function(x){

  list(
    mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd   = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

}

trad_stats <- lapply(
  train_dt[, ..trad_numeric],
  std_from_train
)

tele_stats <- lapply(
  train_dt[, ..telematics_selected],
  std_from_train
)

###################################################
# SCALING FUNCTION
###################################################

scale_block <- function(data, vars, stats){

  m <- sapply(vars, function(v){

    (data[[v]] - stats[[v]]$mean) /
      stats[[v]]$sd

  })

  m <- as.matrix(m)

  colnames(m) <- vars

  m
}

###################################################
# BRANCH 1 : GLM/TRADITIONAL VARIABLES
###################################################

f_trad <- ~

  Insured.sex +
  Marital +
  Region +
  Car.use.grp +

  Insured.age +
  Car.age +
  Years.noclaims +
  Credit.score

X_trad_train <- model.matrix(
  f_trad,
  data = train_dt
)

X_trad_test <- model.matrix(
  f_trad,
  data = test_dt
)

###################################################
# BRANCH 2 : TELEMATICS VARIABLES
###################################################

X_tele_train <- scale_block(
  train_dt,
  telematics_selected,
  tele_stats
)

X_tele_test <- scale_block(
  test_dt,
  telematics_selected,
  tele_stats
)

###################################################
# TARGET
###################################################

y_train <- train_dt$NB_Claim
y_test  <- test_dt$NB_Claim

###################################################
# OFFSET
###################################################

offset_train <- log(train_dt$Exposure)
offset_test  <- log(test_dt$Exposure)

###################################################
# GLM COEFFICIENTS FOR WARM START
###################################################

beta_glm <- coef(mod_full_nb)

###################################################
# CHECKS
###################################################

cat(
  "X_trad_train:",
  dim(X_trad_train),
  "\n"
)

cat(
  "X_tele_train:",
  dim(X_tele_train),
  "\n"
)

cat(
  "Length y_train:",
  length(y_train),
  "\n"
)

cat(
  "Length beta_glm:",
  length(beta_glm),
  "\n"
)

###################################################
# VERIFY DESIGN MATRIX VS GLM
###################################################

names(beta_glm)

colnames(X_trad_train)
```
